flashcards.q: What question does GRASP answer that SOLID doesn't?
flashcards.a: GRASP answers who/which object should own a responsibility (Information Expert, Creator, Controller...); SOLID answers how a class already assigned a responsibility should be shaped.

flashcards.q: What is the narrow, original definition of DRY (Pragmatic Programmer, 1999)?
flashcards.a: Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation — not 'never write similar-looking code twice'.
Code that is identical today because it happens to solve two unrelated problems the same way right now, not because it represents shared business knowledge; merging it creates false coupling.

flashcards.q: What is the Rule of Three?
flashcards.a: Tolerate duplication through the second occurrence; only extract a shared abstraction on the third, once the actual shared shape is visible rather than guessed at.

flashcards.q: What does KISS actually argue against, and what does it NOT license removing?
flashcards.a: It argues against unnecessary structural complexity (extra layers/abstraction/generality) for the same guarantees; it does not license removing correctness guarantees like validation or bounds checks.

flashcards.q: Where does YAGNI fail as an organizational strategy even though each team applies it correctly?
flashcards.a: Cross-team shared infrastructure (schema registry, idempotency conventions) — every team correctly skips building it individually, and in aggregate nobody builds it until multiple teams need it simultaneously during an incident.
A method should only call methods on: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, or its direct components — not on objects returned by those calls ('don't talk to strangers').

flashcards.q: When does strict Law of Demeter application become counterproductive?
flashcards.a: Inside a single cohesive aggregate that changes as a unit — forcing one-hop-only rules produces wrapper explosion (forwarding methods everywhere) with no real encapsulation benefit.

flashcards.q: What GRASP pattern names inventing a non-domain class purely for cohesion/coupling reasons?
flashcards.a: Pure Fabrication — e.g. a PricingEngine that isn't a real business concept but keeps pricing logic out of the Order entity.

flashcards.q: Why does Penguin extends Bird with fly() throwing an exception violate both LSP and composition-over-inheritance guidance?
flashcards.a: It models 'is-a' for taxonomy when callers depend on behavior; the fix (inject a FlightBehavior strategy) is the same technique that fixes LSP violations and OCP's strategy pattern.

flashcards.q: Which languages structurally forbid classical inheritance and lean on composition by design?
flashcards.a: Go and Rust — Go via embedding/interfaces, Rust via traits/generics, both avoiding classical inheritance hierarchies entirely.

flashcards.q: Who formalized GRASP and in what work?
flashcards.a: Craig Larman, in Applying UML and Patterns (1997).
